newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: WTO finance pact good for Seoul, U.S. says.
newsitem.headline: WTO finance pact good for Seoul, U.S. says.

text.p: South Korea has much to gain and nothing to lose by submitting an "ambitious offer" to open its financial markets, deputy U.S. Trade Representative Jeffrey Lang said on Tuesday.
A U.S. delegation led by Lang visited various South Korean ministries on a swing through Asia to lobby for a pact liberalising financial services.

The World Trade Organisation, the Geneva-based body that promotes free trade, faces a December 12 deadline to reach an agreement deregulating financial services. An interim WTO accord on financial services expires at the end of this year.
"We made the point that Korea's participation in WTO financial services is absolutely critical. We're gratified that everyone we talked to agreed on that point," Lang told reporters.
South Korean officials indicated Seoul's offer on opening its financial services sector would be submitted to the WTO at the end of August or early in September, he said.
The United States has already promised to back a WTO financial services pact by offering substantially full market access to foreign firms in the domestic financial sector.
Lang said he would not discuss specifics of what might be in South Korea's offer, but said the Koreans, "in general, seem to agree with the basic principles" of market opening.
"We've made our views on what would be in our mutual interest very clear to our friends here in Seoul," Lang said.
Lang also said there was no inconsistency between market-opening efforts in financial services and the safety and stability of world financial markets.
"In fact, we think the two things may be mutually reinforcing," Lang said.
A senior treasury department official travelling with Lang said the U.S. position was that "financial tensions" in the region were not the result of market liberalisation.

Thailand is in the midst of a financial crisis, with its currency regularly hitting new lows against the dollar. Currency speculation has also hit Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines, giving rise to concerns that financial reforms had exacerbated some of their troubles.
In a letter to the head of the WTO released on Monday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said the United States would work creatively to deal with the concerns of emerging economies.

"We want to consider with our negotiating partners phased commitments, over agreed timeframes appropriate to a country's circumstances, as well as other measures which we believe can smooth the transition to a more economic environment," Rubin wrote.

Financial services covers banking, securities business, insurance, asset management and linked activities. The WTO says the financial services sector accounts for $1.2 trillion a day in foreign exchange transactions around the globe.
